title: Cloud security and IAM
summary: Cloud security from identity up: AWS IAM policies and how they are evaluated, roles and keyless federation, IMDSv2, public storage, KMS, logging and response, with Azure and GCP mapped and real breaches.
outcomes: Explain the shared responsibility model and place any control on the provider's or the customer's side
Read an IAM policy and predict how AWS evaluates a request across explicit denies, SCPs, boundaries and resource policies
Replace wildcard policies and long-lived keys with least-privilege roles, STS sessions and OIDC federation from CI
Harden instance credentials with IMDSv2 everywhere and a VPC-based data perimeter
Find and close public storage: S3 Block Public Access, Azure SAS tokens and Google public access prevention
Map AWS IAM ideas to Azure RBAC, managed identities and Google Cloud IAM
Recognise key abuse in CloudTrail and respond to a leaked cloud key step by step
Use Capital One, Uber, Microsoft's SAS token, Snowflake, ChaosDB and OMIGOD to explain how cloud breaches happen

lessons.title: The cloud from a security view: computers you rent through an API

blocks.md:
Ana runs the website for a small shop. Ten years ago that meant buying a server and putting it in a rack. Today Ana types one command, and a few seconds later a virtual machine exists in a data centre Ana will never see, billed by the second. Deleting it is one more command. Anyone who holds Ana's credentials can type those same commands, from anywhere.

That is the security story of this course in one paragraph. The cloud is other people's computers that you control entirely through an API (application programming interface: a set of requests one program can send another). Whoever can make those requests with valid credentials controls your infrastructure.

NIST (the National Institute of Standards and Technology, the US standards body) defines cloud computing in SP 800-145 as "a model for enabling ubiquitous, convenient, on-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources ... that can be rapidly provisioned and released with minimal management effort or service provider interaction." The same document names five essential characteristics, four deployment models and three service models:

- **IaaS** (Infrastructure as a Service): you rent virtual machines, disks and networks and run everything on top.
- **PaaS** (Platform as a Service): you hand over code and the provider runs it.
- **SaaS** (Software as a Service): you use finished software, such as email or a data warehouse.

The three biggest providers are AWS (Amazon Web Services), Microsoft Azure and GCP (Google Cloud Platform). In the security job postings DevDump sampled, about 45% asked for AWS, 36% for GCP and 30% for Azure, so this course teaches AWS in depth and maps each idea to the other two.

AWS splits most services into two halves:

- The **control plane** is the administrative API: create, describe, update, delete and list resources. Launching a VM (virtual machine) or creating a storage bucket is a control plane action.
- The **data plane** is the service doing its job: the running VM, or getting and putting files in a bucket.

Both are reached over HTTPS. AWS's policy documentation says the same thing about every entry point: whether a person uses the web console, the CLI (command line interface) or the API, "that principal sends a request to AWS", and AWS decides whether to allow it. The console is just a friendly client for the same API.

blocks.code:
# Who am I? (works from any laptop that holds the credentials)
aws sts get-caller-identity

# Control plane: create a bucket in Amazon S3
aws s3api create-bucket --bucket example-reports-bucket --region us-east-1

# Data plane: put a file into it, then read it back
aws s3 cp q3.csv s3://example-reports-bucket/q3.csv
aws s3 cp s3://example-reports-bucket/q3.csv -
blocks.caption: Three kinds of request, one credential. S3 is Amazon Simple Storage Service (the three S's of its name); a bucket is a named container of files, called objects.

blocks.title: Every path into the cloud ends at the same identity check

scenes.caption: Ana's laptop sends a signed request to the AWS API. The endpoint authenticates the signature, then IAM decides whether this identity may do this action on this resource.
The CI pipeline (continuous integration: the robot that builds and deploys code) uses the same API with its own credentials. There is no separate back door for automation.
A stranger holding a copy of Ana's key sends a byte-for-byte valid request from another continent. The endpoint is on the public internet, so no office firewall sits in the path.
So the only gate is the identity check: which credentials, and what those credentials are allowed to do. Identity and configuration are the perimeter.

blocks.md: In the cloud every resource is managed through a public API, so whoever holds valid credentials can act from anywhere. The main walls are identities, permissions and configuration, not the office network.

This is why the DevDump security curriculum describes cloud breaches as "mostly identity and configuration: IAM policies, metadata services and storage exposure". IAM (Identity and Access Management) is the system that says who may do what; you met its general form as authorization in the access control course. The real cases in this course follow that pattern: AWS keys found in a code repository (Uber, 2016), an over-permissioned server role (Capital One, 2019), an over-broad storage link (Microsoft, 2023) and stolen passwords without MFA (Snowflake customers, 2024). A few, such as ChaosDB and OMIGOD in 2021, were bugs on the provider's side, and we will see what customers could still do.

blocks.question: Which of these is a data plane action in AWS's terms?
options: Downloading an object from a bucket
Changing a bucket's access policy
Creating a new S3 bucket
Launching a new virtual machine
blocks.explain: The data plane is the service doing its job, such as getting and putting objects. Creating buckets, changing their policies and launching VMs are administrative control plane actions.

blocks.question: Ana's access key leaked in a public chat. The company's office firewall blocks all inbound traffic. What can a stranger who copied the key do?
options: Nothing, because the firewall blocks them
Anything the key's permissions allow, from any internet connection, because the AWS API is a public endpoint
Only read data, because writes need the console
Only act from inside the office network
blocks.explain: The AWS API is reached over the internet and the console uses the same API. A valid key works from anywhere; only the key's permissions and any conditions in policies limit it.

lessons.title: The shared responsibility model, and when the provider gets it wrong

blocks.md:
Think of renting a flat. The landlord keeps the roof sound and locks the building's front door. You lock your own flat, decide who gets a copy of your key, and do not leave the window open. If a burglar climbs through your open window, the landlord's excellent front door did not help.

AWS calls its version the **shared responsibility model**: AWS is responsible for "security *of* the cloud" (the hardware, software, networking and facilities that run its services), and the customer for "security *in* the cloud". Microsoft and Google publish the same idea under similar names.

Where the line falls depends on the service. AWS's own two examples:

- **Amazon EC2** (Elastic Compute Cloud, the two C's; elastic because capacity grows and shrinks on demand) is IaaS. The customer manages "the guest operating system (including updates and security patches), any application software or utilities installed by the customer on the instances, and the configuration of the AWS-provided firewall (called a security group)".
- For abstracted services such as **Amazon S3**, AWS runs the infrastructure, operating system and platform. Customers remain "responsible for managing their data (including encryption options), classifying their assets, and using IAM tools to apply the appropriate permissions."

Notice what never moves to the provider: your data, your identities and who you grant access to.

blocks.title: Who is responsible for what (0 = provider, 1 = customer)

scenes.caption: Simplified from AWS's description. Rows are layers of a system; columns are three kinds of service. A 1 means the customer must get it right.
EC2 (IaaS): the customer patches the guest operating system, runs the application and writes the security group rules. Only the building, hardware and virtualization layer are AWS's.
S3 and a SaaS product such as Snowflake: the provider runs everything up to the service itself. The customer still sets network allow rules, data handling and permissions.
The bottom two rows are 1 in every column. However much you outsource, data, identities and permissions stay yours. Most cloud breaches in this course live in these rows.

blocks.md: **Snowflake customers, 2024.** Snowflake is a cloud data warehouse (SaaS). Mandiant (Google's incident response firm) investigated a campaign by a group it tracks as UNC5537 (UNC: Mandiant's label for an uncategorized group) and found no evidence that access "stemmed from a breach of Snowflake's enterprise environment". Every incident traced back to customer credentials stolen by infostealer malware (programs that copy saved passwords off infected computers), the oldest from an infection in November 2020. The affected accounts had no MFA (multi-factor authentication), many passwords had not been rotated for years (in some cases four), and there were no network allow lists limiting where logins could come from. Mandiant and Snowflake notified about 165 potentially exposed organizations. Each missing control sits in the customer's rows of the matrix.

The provider's side does fail sometimes, and two 2021 bugs show what that looks like.

**ChaosDB.** Azure Cosmos DB is Microsoft's globally distributed database service. Researchers Sagi Tzadik and Nir Ohfeld of Wiz (a cloud security company) found that its Jupyter Notebook feature (Jupyter: an interactive notebook for running code in the browser) let code escalate to root inside the notebook container. As root they could delete the container's local firewall rules, which had been the only thing keeping them from internal addresses, and from there obtain keys that unlocked other customers' databases. Microsoft says the report arrived on August 12, 2021, that it disabled the feature, and that it told affected customers to regenerate their primary read-write keys.

**[OMIGOD](https://www.wiz.io/blog/omigod-critical-vulnerabilities-in-omi-azure).** OMI (Open Management Infrastructure) is an open-source management agent that several Azure VM management extensions install on Linux VMs. Wiz reported that it was "almost completely undocumented" for customers, many of whom did not know it was running, and that over 65% of sampled Azure customers were exposed. The worst of four bugs, CVE-2021-38647 (CVE: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, the public ID system for bugs), let a request with no `Authorization` header run commands as root, because missing authentication left the user id at 0, which on Linux means root. It was remotely reachable when OMI's management ports (5985, 5986, 1270) were exposed. Microsoft [released fixes](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/msrc/blog/2021/09/additional-guidance-regarding-omi-vulnerabilities-within-azure-vm-management-extensions) on September 14, 2021 and updated extensions it managed; customers who had installed OMI themselves had to update it.

blocks.caption: The vulnerable version only checks credentials when they are present, so leaving them out skips the check and keeps the most powerful default. The fix treats a missing header as a failed login.

blocks.md: Common misconception: "we are on a big cloud, so the provider handles security." The provider secures its platform. Your identities, keys, data and configuration are yours, and even provider-side bugs usually ended with a customer to-do: regenerate keys after ChaosDB, update agents after OMIGOD.

blocks.question: A company stores files in S3. Which task is the company's responsibility, not AWS's?
options: Replacing failed disks
Patching the operating system of the servers that run S3
Physically guarding the data centre
Deciding which identities may read the bucket and whether objects are encrypted with a key it manages
blocks.explain: For abstracted services AWS runs the infrastructure, operating system and platform. Data handling, encryption choices and IAM permissions stay with the customer.

blocks.question: Mandiant found that the 2024 Snowflake data thefts used stolen passwords on accounts without MFA or network allow lists. Where does that fall in the shared responsibility model?
options: On the infostealer authors only
Nowhere, because SaaS has no shared responsibility
On Snowflake's side, because Snowflake runs the software
On the customer's side: identities and access rules are always the customer's
blocks.explain: Even for SaaS, the customer decides who has accounts, whether MFA is required and where logins may come from. Mandiant found no breach of Snowflake's own environment.

blocks.question: After ChaosDB, what did Microsoft ask potentially affected Cosmos DB customers to do?
options: Nothing, the provider fixed it entirely
Delete their databases
Regenerate their primary read-write keys
Disable Azure Active Directory
blocks.explain: Microsoft disabled the notebook feature and asked customers whose keys might have been exposed to regenerate the primary read-write key. A provider bug still left a credential that only the customer could rotate.

lessons.title: Accounts, subscriptions and projects: the boxes everything lives in

blocks.md:
Before you can say who may do what, you need to know where things live. A small company might start with one AWS account holding everything. A year later it has production, staging, a developer sandbox and a place for logs, and putting all of them in one box means one leaked developer key can touch production.

So every cloud has a container that is both a billing unit and a security boundary, and a way to group those containers under one owner. The names differ, but the shape is the same.

**AWS.** An **AWS account** holds resources and identities. It is created with an email address that becomes the **root user**, which AWS's evaluation rules exempt from the usual default deny: it "has full access". That is why AWS advises locking the root user away with MFA and using it almost never; an organization can now also remove member accounts' root credentials entirely (centralized root access management).

**AWS Organizations** groups accounts under one **management account**, with **member accounts** arranged into **OUs** (organizational units, folders of accounts) and a single consolidated bill. The organization can attach **SCPs** (service control policies) to OUs or accounts. An SCP "never grants permissions"; it sets a guardrail, an upper limit on what any user or role in the account may do, and it applies even to a member account's root user. Two exceptions matter: SCPs do not affect the management account, and they do not affect service-linked roles (roles AWS services use on your behalf).

**Azure.** People and apps live in a **Microsoft Entra ID** tenant (Entra ID is the renamed Azure Active Directory; Microsoft renamed it partly to avoid confusion with Windows Server Active Directory). Resources live in a hierarchy: **management groups**, then **subscriptions** (the billing and isolation unit), then **resource groups**, then resources. A role can be assigned at any of those four scopes and is inherited by everything below.

**Google Cloud.** The **organization** resource is the root, then **folders**, then **projects** (the unit that holds resources and billing), then resources. Google's documentation says policies applied at the organization level "are inherited by every resource in the organization".

blocks.title: One owner, many boxes: where a guardrail lands

scenes.caption: An AWS organization: a management account at the top, OUs for production and development, and member accounts inside them. A separate account holds the logs.
An SCP that denies stopping CloudTrail (AWS's API audit log, lesson 14) is attached to the Prod OU. It flows down to every account inside, including those accounts' root users.
The management account is not limited by SCPs at all. That is why it should run almost nothing and have very few people with access.
Logs are shipped to their own account. An attacker who takes over a production account cannot quietly delete the evidence, because they hold no permissions in the log account.

blocks.caption: An SCP is written in the same JSON policy language as IAM policies (next lesson). This one stops anyone in the affected accounts, root user included, from turning off the audit trail or taking the account out of the organization.

blocks.md: Separate accounts (or subscriptions, or projects) are the strongest blast-radius limit the cloud gives you. A key that only exists in the sandbox account cannot touch production, whatever its policies say, unless something in production explicitly trusts it.

blocks.question: A security team attaches an SCP that denies `s3:DeleteBucket` to the Prod OU. An administrator signed in to the organization's management account deletes a bucket in the management account. What happens?
options: The delete succeeds, because SCPs do not affect the management account
The delete is denied by the SCP
The delete is denied because SCPs apply to all accounts in the organization
The delete is queued for approval
blocks.explain: SCPs apply to member accounts below where they are attached. AWS documents that SCPs do not affect users or roles in the management account, which is one reason to keep workloads out of it.

blocks.question: Which statement about an SCP is correct?
options: It only applies to IAM users, not roles
It replaces IAM policies in member accounts
It sets the maximum permissions for principals in the accounts it applies to, and grants nothing on its own
It grants permissions to every user in the account
blocks.explain: An SCP is a guardrail. A request must be allowed by both the SCP and the principal's own policies, and an explicit deny in the SCP wins. It applies to users and roles, including the member account's root user.

lessons.title: IAM from zero: users, groups, roles and the JSON policy

blocks.md:
Start with a tiny example. Ana, an analyst, needs to read quarterly reports from one bucket. Ana should not be able to delete them, and should not touch the payroll bucket at all. In AWS that sentence becomes three things: an **identity** for Ana, a **policy** saying what is allowed, and the **resources** the policy names.

IAM (Identity and Access Management) is the AWS service that holds all three. In the access control course you met the general model: a subject asks to perform an action on an object, and a policy answers allow or deny. IAM is that model, expressed in JSON (JavaScript Object Notation, a plain-text format for structured data).

The kinds of identity, called **principals** when they make requests:

- **Root user**: the account's original email login, with full access. Use it almost never.
- **IAM user**: one person or program, with a console password and/or **access keys** (a long-term key pair). AWS now recommends IAM users only when nothing else works.
- **IAM group**: a set of users that share policies. A group is not a principal: AWS says groups "relate to permissions, not authentication", so you cannot name a group in a policy's `Principal`, and groups cannot be nested.
- **IAM role**: an identity with permissions but no long-term credentials. People, services or other accounts **assume** it and receive temporary credentials. Roles are the backbone of good cloud security, and lessons 7 to 9 are about them.

Every resource has an **ARN** (Amazon Resource Name), a globally unique string: `arn:partition:service:region:account-id:resource`. Examples: `arn:aws:iam::111122223333:user/ana` (IAM is global, so region is empty; a Region is one of AWS's separate geographic locations, such as us-east-1 in northern Virginia, and most resources live in exactly one) and `arn:aws:s3:::reports-bucket/q3.csv` (bucket names are global, so region and account are empty).

Policies come in two main kinds. An **identity-based policy** is attached to a user, group or role and says what that identity may do. A **resource-based policy** is attached to a resource, such as an S3 bucket policy, and also names **who** (`Principal`) may act on it. Lesson 5 adds the guardrail types: SCPs, permissions boundaries and session policies.

blocks.caption: An identity-based policy for Ana. Version 2012-10-17 is the current policy language version, and AWS says to always include it. Each statement has an Effect, a list of Actions, the Resources they apply to and an optional Condition.

blocks.md:
Reading a statement:

- **Effect** is `Allow` or `Deny`.
- **Action** names API operations as `service:Operation`, and may use the wildcard `*`: `s3:Get*` matches every S3 operation starting with Get, and `s3:*` matches all of S3.
- **Resource** lists ARNs the statement covers, also with wildcards (`*` for any characters, `?` for one). Note the pair above: `s3:ListBucket` acts on the bucket ARN, `s3:GetObject` on object ARNs ending `/*`. Getting this pairing wrong is a very common reason a correct-looking policy does not work.
- **Condition** adds tests on the request context, using operators such as `StringEquals`, `StringLike`, `IpAddress` and `Bool`, and keys such as `aws:SourceIp`, `aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent`, `aws:SecureTransport` (was HTTPS used) or `aws:PrincipalOrgID` (is the caller in my organization).

blocks.title: Matching one request against Ana's policy

scenes.caption: The request: Ana, signed in with MFA, calls s3:GetObject on reports-bucket/q3.csv. AWS walks every statement looking for ones that match.
Statement ReadReports: the action is in the list, so keep checking.
The resource matches the object pattern reports-bucket/*.
The condition requires MFA on this session. It is present, so this statement contributes an Allow.
Statement NeverDeleteReports covers DeleteObject only, so it does not apply. One Allow and no Deny: the request is allowed.
Same request without MFA: the condition fails, so ReadReports does not match. Nothing allows it, which means the default deny wins.
scenes.output: GetObject without MFA: denied (no matching Allow)

scenes.caption: Ana tries DeleteObject. ReadReports does not list it, and NeverDeleteReports explicitly denies it. An explicit Deny can never be overridden by an Allow anywhere.

blocks.md: IAM starts from deny. A request is allowed only if some applicable policy explicitly allows it and no applicable policy explicitly denies it. Write policies as a list of what is needed, never as a list of what to forbid.

blocks.question: A policy allows `s3:ListBucket` on `arn:aws:s3:::reports-bucket/*` only. Ana runs a listing of the bucket and is denied. Why?
options: Wildcards are not allowed in Resource
ListBucket acts on the bucket itself, so the Resource must be `arn:aws:s3:::reports-bucket`, not the object pattern
Listing always needs the root user
ListBucket needs MFA
blocks.explain: Bucket-level operations such as ListBucket apply to the bucket ARN; object operations such as GetObject apply to object ARNs ending in /*. A mismatched pair matches nothing, so the default deny wins.

blocks.question: Which of these can appear in the `Principal` element of a bucket policy?
options: An IAM group
An IAM role ARN
An OU name
A security group
blocks.explain: Principals are authenticated identities such as users, roles, accounts and services. Groups only collect permissions for users and cannot be principals.

lessons.title: How AWS decides: explicit deny, SCPs, boundaries and resource policies

blocks.md:
One request can be covered by many policies at once: an SCP from the organization, the role's own identity policy, a permissions boundary, the bucket's policy. Which one wins? Picture a building with a guard at the street gate (the organization), a receptionist (your own badge's permissions) and a lock on the room (the resource). A single "no entry" sign anywhere stops you, and you need a yes from each checkpoint that applies.

AWS documents this as its policy evaluation logic. It is worth learning precisely, because almost every cloud permission bug and every cloud guardrail depends on it.

The rules from AWS's documentation, for a request inside one account:

1. **Default deny.** "By default, all requests are implicitly denied", except for the root user.
2. **Explicit deny wins.** AWS first searches every applicable policy (SCPs, RCPs (step 3), resource-based, identity-based, permissions boundaries, session policies) for a `Deny` that matches. "If the enforcement code finds even one explicit deny that applies," the answer is Deny.
3. **Organization guardrails.** If the account is in an organization, an applicable **RCP** (resource control policy, an organization guardrail on resources) and **SCP** must each allow the action, or the answer is Deny.
4. **Resource-based policy.** Within one account, a resource policy that grants access directly to the calling user or role session can allow the request even if the identity policy says nothing.
5. **Identity-based policy.** Otherwise some identity policy must allow it.
6. **Permissions boundary and session policy.** If the principal has a boundary, or the session was created with a session policy, those must also allow it.

Two of these are new. A **permissions boundary** is a managed policy attached to a user or role that sets "the maximum permissions that an identity-based policy can grant". It grants nothing itself: the effective permissions are the intersection of the identity policy and the boundary. Teams use it to let developers create roles for their apps without being able to create a role more powerful than a fixed limit.

A **session policy** is an optional policy passed when you request temporary credentials, which narrows that one session further.

**Across accounts** the rule tightens: the caller's identity policy in its own account and the resource's policy in the other account must both allow the request.

blocks.title: The evaluation order, applied to four requests

scenes.caption: Request 1: a role calls s3:GetObject on reports-bucket/q3.csv. No Deny matches, the SCP allows everything, the identity policy allows this bucket, there is no boundary: Allow.
Request 2: the same role reads payroll-bucket/salaries.csv. Nothing denies it, but nothing allows it either. The identity step finds no Allow, so the default deny stands.
Request 3: the role calls cloudtrail:StopLogging. Its identity policy allows cloudtrail:*, but the SCP has an explicit Deny, and that is checked first. Allow elsewhere cannot save it.
Request 4: a developer's role has s3:* on everything, but a permissions boundary allows only s3:GetObject. A DeleteObject call passes the identity step and fails at the boundary.

blocks.md: The diagram is simplified: it merges the identity and resource policy steps and leaves out the exceptions for role trust policies and KMS (Key Management Service, lesson 12) key policies, which must always explicitly allow the caller. The short Python model below follows the same order so you can test your intuition. It is a teaching model, not AWS's code: real action names match case-insensitively, conditions are skipped, and resource policies are left out.

blocks.title: A simplified evaluator in Python
blocks.code:
from fnmatch import fnmatchcase

def matches(stmt, action, resource):
    acts = stmt["Action"] if isinstance(stmt["Action"], list) else [stmt["Action"]]
    ress = stmt["Resource"] if isinstance(stmt["Resource"], list) else [stmt["Resource"]]
    return (any(fnmatchcase(action, a) for a in acts)
            and any(fnmatchcase(resource, r) for r in ress))

def effects(policies, action, resource):
    return {s["Effect"] for p in policies for s in p["Statement"]
            if matches(s, action, resource)}

def decide(req, scps, identity, boundary=None):
    a, r = req["action"], req["resource"]
    every = scps + identity + (boundary or [])
    if "Deny" in effects(every, a, r):
        return "Deny (explicit)"
    if scps and "Allow" not in effects(scps, a, r):
        return "Deny (no SCP allow)"
    if "Allow" not in effects(identity, a, r):
        return "Deny (implicit)"
    if boundary and "Allow" not in effects(boundary, a, r):
        return "Deny (boundary)"
    return "Allow"

scp = [{"Statement": [
    {"Effect": "Allow", "Action": "*", "Resource": "*"},
    {"Effect": "Deny", "Action": "cloudtrail:StopLogging", "Resource": "*"}]}]
role = [{"Statement": [
    {"Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject"],
     "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::reports-bucket/*"},
    {"Effect": "Allow", "Action": "cloudtrail:*", "Resource": "*"}]}]

for action, resource in [
        ("s3:GetObject", "arn:aws:s3:::reports-bucket/q3.csv"),
        ("s3:GetObject", "arn:aws:s3:::payroll-bucket/salaries.csv"),
        ("cloudtrail:StopLogging", "arn:aws:cloudtrail:us-east-1:111122223333:trail/main")]:
    print(action, resource.split(":::")[-1], decide(
        {"action": action, "resource": resource}, scp, role))

scenes.caption: One SCP allows everything except stopping CloudTrail. The role may read and write reports-bucket objects and do anything in CloudTrail.
Request 1: GetObject on reports-bucket/q3.csv. The function first collects the effects of every matching statement in every policy. None is a Deny.
The SCP's Allow * matches and the role's statement matches reports-bucket/*, so the request is allowed.
Request 2: payroll-bucket. The SCP allows it, but no identity statement names that bucket. With no Allow, the function returns an implicit deny.
Request 3: StopLogging. The role's cloudtrail:* matches, but so does the SCP's Deny. The Deny check runs first and ends the evaluation.

blocks.prompt: A role's identity policy allows only `s3:GetObject`. Its permissions boundary allows `s3:*`. Can the role call `s3:PutObject`?
blocks.reveal: No. A boundary sets a ceiling and grants nothing. The effective permission is the intersection of the identity policy (GetObject) and the boundary (all of S3), which is just GetObject. Running the model above with these two policies prints `Deny (implicit)` for PutObject.

blocks.md: "We added an Allow, so it should work" is the classic debugging trap. If anything anywhere has a matching `Deny`, including an SCP you cannot see from inside the account, no Allow will help. AWS's documentation advises asking your organization's administrators when an SCP might be the cause.

blocks.question: An identity policy allows `ec2:*`. An SCP on the account allows only `s3:*` and `iam:*` (it has no other Allow). What happens when the role calls `ec2:RunInstances`?
options: Denied, because the SCP has no Allow for EC2, even though it has no explicit Deny
Denied only if a permissions boundary also exists
Allowed, because the identity policy allows it
Allowed, because SCPs only contain Deny statements
blocks.explain: An action must be allowed by every SCP that applies. If the SCPs contain no matching Allow, AWS returns Deny before it looks at the identity policy.

blocks.question: Within one account, a bucket policy grants `s3:GetObject` directly to the IAM user `ana`. Ana's identity policies say nothing about S3, and Ana has no boundary. What happens?
options: Denied, because bucket policies only apply to other accounts
Allowed only if the request uses MFA
Allowed, because within one account a resource policy that names the user can grant access by itself
Denied, because the identity policy has no Allow
blocks.explain: AWS documents that within the same account, a resource-based policy that grants permission directly to the requesting IAM user or role session is not limited by an implicit deny in identity policies. Across accounts both sides would need to allow it.

lessons.title: Least privilege, wildcards and the Capital One role

blocks.md:
A hotel cleaner needs to enter the rooms on one floor during the day. Giving them the master key for the whole building works too, and nobody notices the difference until the key is stolen. Then it matters enormously.

**Least privilege**, one of the design principles Jerome Saltzer and Michael Schroeder listed in 1975 (you met it in the access control course), says every program and user should run with the least set of privileges needed for the job. In the cloud it has a very concrete form: the `Action` and `Resource` lines of every policy. Two asterisks, one after `Action` and one after `Resource`, are the difference between "write logs to one folder" and "do anything to any bucket in the account".

blocks.caption: Vulnerable: every S3 action on every bucket. If the workload holding this policy is ever tricked or its credentials copied, every bucket in the account is readable, writable and deletable.
Least privilege for a component that only writes its own logs: one action, one prefix in one bucket. It cannot list buckets, read anything or delete anything.

blocks.md:
**Capital One, 2019, from the IAM side.** The server-side web attacks course told the story of the attack: a misconfigured WAF (web application firewall) relayed an outsider's request to the instance metadata service, which returned the temporary credentials of the role attached to the WAF's server. That SSRF (server-side request forgery) opened the door. The role decided how big the room was.

KrebsOnSecurity (the news site of security journalist Brian Krebs), citing a source with knowledge of the investigation, reported that the WAF "was assigned too many permissions, i.e. it was allowed to list all of the files in any buckets of data, and to read the contents of each of those files." A firewall needs to write its own logs. It did not need to read the credit card application data of about 106 million people (100 million in the US, 6 million in Canada), which is what [Capital One says](https://www.capitalone.com/digital/facts2019/) was taken.

blocks.title: A role as broad as s3:* (1 = allowed)

scenes.caption: Before: a role with s3:* on everything. The reported Capital One role could list and read every bucket; write and delete show what s3:* adds. Names invented; ListAllMyBuckets is account-wide.
Stolen credentials carry exactly these permissions. Listing and reading the customer-data column is all it takes to copy it out, from anywhere on the internet.
After: the role may only put objects into its own log bucket. The same stolen credentials now let an attacker write log files, and nothing else.

blocks.caption: The same fix in Terraform (HashiCorp's infrastructure-as-code tool, lesson 15). It assumes a role resource named app and a bucket resource named reports defined elsewhere in the same configuration.

blocks.md:
Watch especially for **IAM write actions**. A principal that may call `iam:AttachUserPolicy` or `iam:CreatePolicyVersion` on itself can give itself any permission, and one that may call `iam:PassRole` for a powerful role plus `ec2:RunInstances` can start a server that runs with that role. AWS describes PassRole as the control that ensures "only approved users can configure a service with a role that grants permissions". Treat these actions as administrator rights.

Tools that help:

- **IAM Access Analyzer** can generate a least-privilege policy from the actions a role actually used, recorded in CloudTrail (the AWS audit log, lesson 14), and flag resources shared publicly or with other accounts.
- **Last accessed information** shows which services a user or role has not used, so you can remove them.

`"Resource": "*"` is not always a mistake (a few actions, such as `s3:ListAllMyBuckets`, have no narrower resource), but `"Action": "*"` or `"service:*"` on `"Resource": "*"` in an application's role almost always is. Treat each one as a finding that needs a written reason.

blocks.question: A role used only by a log shipper has `"Action": "s3:*", "Resource": "*"`. An SSRF bug leaks its credentials. Which change most reduces the damage?
options: Rotate the role's credentials every day
Scope the policy to `s3:PutObject` on the log bucket's prefix
Add a second statement allowing `s3:GetObject`
Rename the buckets to random names
blocks.explain: Role credentials already rotate automatically. What the attacker can do with stolen credentials is exactly what the policy allows, so shrinking Action and Resource shrinks the breach.

blocks.question: Which permission effectively makes a principal an administrator, even if the rest of its policy looks narrow?
options: s3:GetObject on one bucket
iam:AttachUserPolicy on its own user
ec2:DescribeInstances
cloudwatch:GetMetricData
blocks.explain: A principal that can attach policies to itself can attach AdministratorAccess. IAM write actions, and PassRole for powerful roles, deserve the same scrutiny as admin rights.

lessons.title: Long-lived keys vs temporary credentials: STS and Uber 2016

blocks.md:
Compare a copied house key with a hotel key card. The house key works until you change the locks, which most people never do. The key card stops working when you check out. If either is stolen, the damage window is "until someone notices" for the first and "until tomorrow at noon" for the second.

AWS has both kinds. An IAM user's **access key** is a pair: an access key ID (public, like a username) and a secret access key (private, used to sign each request). AWS's documented ID prefixes tell them apart: `AKIA` marks a long-term access key, `ASIA` a temporary key from STS (Security Token Service, below). Long-term keys never expire on their own. Temporary credentials add a third part, a **session token**, and stop working at a set time.

**STS** (Security Token Service) issues the temporary kind. Its central call is **AssumeRole**: a principal that already has credentials asks to become a role for a while. Two different policies are involved, and mixing them up is a classic mistake:

- The role's **trust policy** is a resource-based policy on the role saying **who may assume it**. AWS calls it "a required resource-based policy that is attached to a role".
- The role's **permissions policies** say **what the session may do** once assumed. A trust policy that lets another account assume the role (say, a vendor's) should also require an `sts:ExternalId` the vendor agreed with you, so a different customer of that vendor cannot trick it into using your role (the "confused deputy" problem).

The `DurationSeconds` parameter can range from 900 seconds (15 minutes) up to the role's maximum session duration, at most 43,200 seconds (12 hours), and defaults to 3,600 seconds (one hour). Sessions created by role chaining (one role assuming another) are capped at one hour.

blocks.caption: The trust policy on role report-reader: only the scheduler role in the same account may assume it. Nothing here grants S3 access; that lives in the role's separate permissions policy.

blocks.title: AssumeRole: trading one identity for a short-lived one

scenes.caption: The scheduler, already holding its own role credentials, asks STS to assume report-reader for 15 minutes. The request is signed like any other API call.
STS checks the target role's trust policy: is the caller listed as allowed to assume it? It is, so STS mints a new key ID starting ASIA, a secret, a session token and an expiry time.
The app signs an S3 request with the temporary credentials. S3 asks IAM to evaluate the role's permissions policies, exactly as in lesson 5.
Someone copies the temporary credentials from a log file. For the next few minutes they work for the copier too: temporary is not the same as harmless.
After the expiry time, AWS no longer recognizes the credentials. The copier's requests fail, while the real app simply asks STS again.

blocks.code:
import boto3

# No keys in code: boto3 searches its default chain (environment, web
# identity token, config files, container, then the EC2 metadata service).
sts = boto3.client("sts", region_name="us-east-1")

resp = sts.assume_role(
    RoleArn="arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/report-reader",
    RoleSessionName="nightly-report",
    DurationSeconds=900,              # 15 minutes, the minimum
)
creds = resp["Credentials"]           # AccessKeyId starts with ASIA

s3 = boto3.client(
    "s3",
    region_name="us-east-1",
    aws_access_key_id=creds["AccessKeyId"],
    aws_secret_access_key=creds["SecretAccessKey"],
    aws_session_token=creds["SessionToken"],
)
print(creds["AccessKeyId"][:4], creds["Expiration"])
blocks.caption: Python with boto3 (the AWS SDK, software development kit, for Python). No secret appears in the code: the first client finds the app's own credentials through boto3's search order, and the S3 client uses a 15-minute session. Tested against a stubbed STS response, so no real cloud call was made.

blocks.md: **Uber, 2016.** The US FTC (Federal Trade Commission) later laid out what happened. Between October 13 and November 15, 2016, intruders accessed Uber's Amazon S3 datastore "using an AWS access key that was posted to a private GitHub repository". Uber engineers reached the company's GitHub repositories through individual GitHub accounts, generally tied to personal email addresses; Uber had no policy against reusing passwords and did not require MFA on GitHub. The intruders said they got in with passwords exposed in other breaches, found the key, and downloaded sixteen files of unencrypted database backups: about 25.6 million US names and email addresses, 22.1 million names and mobile numbers and 607,000 names and driver's licence numbers. Uber's CEO later [put the worldwide total](https://web.archive.org/web/2017/https://www.uber.com/newsroom/2016-data-incident/) at 57 million users.

It was not the first time. The FTC also describes a 2014 intrusion using an access key that "was publicly posted and granted full administrative privileges" over the same datastore. Every link in the 2016 chain is a lesson of this course: a long-lived key, stored in code, behind a password reused from elsewhere with no MFA, granting broad access to unencrypted data.

Uber learned of the 2016 breach around November 14, 2016, when an attacker demanded a six-figure payment. The FTC says Uber paid USD 100,000 through its bug bounty program's operator and did not tell affected consumers until November 21, 2017, more than a year later. We return to that last failure in the incident response lesson.

blocks.title: How long does a leaked credential stay useful?

scenes.caption: Two credentials in use. The long-term key (AKIA) is valid indefinitely. The app's role sessions are renewed every hour, each one expiring on schedule.
At hour 2.5 both leak into a public place. Session 3 has half an hour left; the key has no end date.
The attacker can use the leaked session until hour 3, then it is dead. The leaked key keeps working until a human finds it and deactivates it, which for Uber in 2016 meant weeks.

blocks.md: Prefer roles and temporary credentials everywhere. AWS's own best practices say to require human users to use federation with temporary credentials and to require workloads to use IAM roles. Long-term access keys are for the few cases nothing else supports, and they need rotation, monitoring and the narrowest possible permissions.

blocks.question: A role's trust policy allows the `ci-deployer` role to assume it, and its permissions policy allows `s3:*`. Which statement is true?
options: The trust policy limits which S3 buckets the session can use
The trust policy lets ci-deployer use S3 directly without assuming the role
ci-deployer can call AssumeRole on it and the resulting session can use S3
Anyone in the account can assume it, because trust policies only apply across accounts
blocks.explain: The trust policy decides who may become the role; the permissions policy decides what the role session may do. Together: ci-deployer may assume it, and the session may use S3.

blocks.question: A log line exposes a key whose ID starts with `ASIA`. What does that tell you?
options: It is the root user's key
It is an EC2 instance ID
It is a long-term IAM user key that never expires
It is a temporary STS credential, which also needs its session token and stops working at its expiry
blocks.explain: AWS documents ASIA as the prefix for temporary STS access keys and AKIA for long-term access keys. A temporary key is only usable with its session token and only until it expires, though that may still be hours.

lessons.title: Instance roles at scale: IMDSv2 everywhere and a data perimeter

blocks.md:
A program on an EC2 instance needs to read a bucket. Pasting a long-term key into its config file is the Uber mistake. The cloud's answer: attach a **role** to the instance and let the program fetch short-lived credentials for it from the machine itself.

The pieces: an **instance profile** is a container that attaches one IAM role to an EC2 instance, and attaching it requires `iam:PassRole` (lesson 6). AWS rotates the role's credentials automatically and serves them from the **IMDS** (Instance Metadata Service) at 169.254.169.254, under `/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/` and the role name. You never write code for this: boto3 searches a fixed list of places for credentials, starting with explicit parameters and environment variables, then web identity tokens and config files, then a container credential provider, and last the instance metadata service, and stops at the first it finds.

The server-side web attacks course covered how this goes wrong and how IMDSv2 answers it: SSRF or an open proxy makes the server fetch its own role credentials (Capital One, 2019); IMDSv2 requires a PUT to open a session and a secret token on every read, refuses tokens to requests carrying `X-Forwarded-For`, and sends the token response with an IP TTL (time to live, a hop counter) of 1 so it cannot leave the machine.

This lesson is the cloud engineer's half of that story: making IMDSv2 the rule across hundreds of accounts, and limiting what stolen role credentials can do even when everything else fails.

blocks.code:
# Require IMDSv2 on an existing instance (AWS CLI)
aws ec2 modify-instance-metadata-options --instance-id i-0123456789abcdef0 --http-tokens required --http-endpoint enabled

# Make IMDSv2 the default for new instances in a Region
aws ec2 modify-instance-metadata-defaults --region us-east-1 --http-tokens required

# Terraform, on the instance resource
metadata_options {
  http_tokens                 = "required" # IMDSv2 only
  http_put_response_hop_limit = 1          # 2 only if containers on the host need IMDS
}
blocks.caption: Three places to require IMDSv2: each running instance, the Region default for new instances (it does not change existing ones), and the infrastructure code that creates them. AWS suggests a hop limit of 2 only when containers on the host need to reach IMDS.

blocks.md:
**A data perimeter for instance credentials.** Even with IMDSv2, some future bug (or code running on the instance) could copy the role's temporary credentials. AWS adds context to every request made with EC2 role credentials: `aws:Ec2InstanceSourceVpc` is the VPC (virtual private cloud, your private network in AWS; lesson 13) the credentials were delivered to. The global key `aws:SourceVpc` is the VPC a request actually came from, and it is present only when the request travels through a VPC endpoint (a private doorway from your VPC to an AWS service, so the traffic never crosses the public internet; lesson 13 shows one).

AWS's documentation gives the policy below, which you can apply as an SCP. It denies any request made with EC2 role credentials unless it comes from the same VPC the credentials were issued into. The `Null` test limits it to instance role credentials, and `aws:ViaAWSService` lets AWS services keep making calls on the instance's behalf (such as S3 calling KMS to decrypt).

blocks.caption: From AWS's documentation of aws:Ec2InstanceSourceVpc. Stolen instance credentials used from an attacker's laptop carry no matching aws:SourceVpc, so this Deny matches.

blocks.title: Stolen instance credentials meet a data perimeter

scenes.caption: The app on the instance gets its role credentials from IMDS with an IMDSv2 token, then reads a report through the VPC's S3 endpoint.
The request carries aws:SourceVpc = vpc-a (it came through the endpoint) and aws:Ec2InstanceSourceVpc = vpc-a (where the credentials were issued). They match, so the Deny does not apply.
Suppose a bug leaks the same credentials and an attacker uses them from home. The signature is valid and the role's own policy allows GetObject.
But the request did not come through the VPC endpoint, so its source VPC does not match vpc-a. The SCP's explicit Deny wins, exactly as in lesson 5.

blocks.md: Roll a perimeter policy out carefully. Because `aws:SourceVpc` exists only for requests through VPC endpoints, any instance role that calls an AWS service over the public internet will start failing. Test in one account first, and check which services each workload calls.

**Defender view.**

- *Prevent:* require IMDSv2 (account defaults plus infrastructure code), keep instance roles least-privilege, and add a data perimeter so instance credentials only work from their own network.
- *Detect:* Amazon GuardDuty (AWS's managed threat detection service, lesson 14) raises an `InstanceCredentialExfiltration.OutsideAWS` finding (default severity High) when instance credentials are used from an external IP address, and its `InsideAWS` twin when they are used from another AWS account. In CloudTrail, an instance role session whose `sourceIPAddress` is not one of your addresses is the signal.
- *Respond:* revoke the role's active sessions (lesson 16), fix the bug that leaked them, and review every call the stolen session made.

blocks.question: A team sets the Region's default to require IMDSv2. A week later an audit finds old instances still answering IMDSv1. Why?
options: Defaults only apply to Windows instances
The account-level default applies to new instances; existing instances keep their own setting until changed
The setting failed silently
IMDSv1 cannot be disabled
blocks.explain: AWS documents that setting the account-level default does not reset existing instances. Each running instance still needs modify-instance-metadata-options, or replacement.

blocks.question: The RequireSameVPC policy is attached as an SCP. An attacker steals an instance role's credentials through an SSRF bug and uses them from a home internet connection. What happens to their S3 calls?
options: They are denied only if MFA is required
They are denied, because the request's source VPC does not match the VPC the credentials were delivered to
They succeed until the credentials expire
They succeed, because the role allows S3
blocks.explain: Requests from outside carry no matching aws:SourceVpc, so the explicit Deny in the SCP applies and overrides the role's Allow. The credentials are valid but useless outside their network.

lessons.title: Keyless pipelines: OIDC from CI, and roles for Kubernetes pods

blocks.md:
A deployment pipeline needs to upload a website to S3. The old way: create an IAM user, generate an access key, paste it into the CI system's secret store. Now a long-lived key sits in a third-party system, readable by anyone who can change the pipeline, forever. In 2021 a tampered uploader script from Codecov (a code coverage service) [copied CI environment variables](https://about.codecov.io/apr-2021-post-mortem/), where such secrets live, to attackers; in 2025 the compromised tj-actions/changed-files action (a reusable step for GitHub Actions, GitHub's built-in CI service) [exposed CI secrets including access keys](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2025/03/18/supply-chain-compromise-third-party-tj-actionschanged-files-cve-2025-30066-and-reviewdogaction).

The modern way stores **no key at all**. The CI system proves who it is with a short-lived signed token, and AWS exchanges that token for temporary role credentials.

The standard underneath is **OIDC** (OpenID Connect), an identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0 in which an identity provider issues signed statements about who someone is. The statement is a **JWT** (JSON Web Token; RFC 7519 suggests pronouncing it like the English word "jot"): a small JSON document signed by the issuer, carrying **claims** such as:

- `iss` (issuer): who signed it, here `https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com`.
- `aud` (audience): who it is meant for, here `sts.amazonaws.com`.
- `sub` (subject): which workload it describes, for GitHub Actions a string like `repo:example-org/shop-site:ref:refs/heads/main`.

You register GitHub's issuer once in IAM as an **OIDC identity provider**, then write a role trust policy that accepts tokens from it, but only with the right claims. STS's `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` call checks the signature and the conditions and returns temporary credentials.

blocks.title: GitHub Actions to AWS without a stored key

scenes.caption: The workflow has permission id-token: write, so the job can ask GitHub's OIDC provider for a token. GitHub signs a JWT whose sub names this repository and branch.
The job sends the JWT to STS and asks to assume the deploy role. No AWS secret exists anywhere in the pipeline.
STS checks GitHub's signature and the role's trust policy: aud must be sts.amazonaws.com and sub must be exactly this repo's main branch. Both match.
The job uploads the site with credentials that expire on their own. There is nothing to rotate and nothing to leak from the CI secret store.
Now a workflow in another repository or branch (same lane, for space) also gets a valid GitHub token, but its sub differs, so the trust policy condition fails.

blocks.caption: The role trust policy, following GitHub's documented pattern. The Federated principal is the registered GitHub provider; the conditions pin the audience and the exact repository and branch.

blocks.code:
name: deploy-site
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  id-token: write   # lets the job request a signed OIDC token
  contents: read

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@e3dd6a429d7300a6a4c196c26e071d42e0343502
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/shop-site-deploy
          role-session-name: shop-site-deploy
          aws-region: us-east-1
      - run: aws s3 cp ./index.html s3://example-site-bucket/
blocks.caption: The workflow: no access key, no secret. The third-party action is pinned to a full commit hash rather than a tag, as GitHub's example does, so a retagged release cannot change what runs.

blocks.md: Never trust the GitHub provider without a `sub` condition: GitHub issues tokens to every repository running Actions, so checking only `aud` accepts workflows you do not control. IAM now rejects new or updated GitHub trust policies without a specific `sub`, though older roles may lack one. Repositories created after July 15, 2026 (or opted in) use immutable subject claims with owner and repository IDs, such as `repo:octo-org@123456/octo-repo@456789:...`, so match your repository's format.

**The same idea inside Kubernetes.** Kubernetes is a system that runs containers across many machines. A **pod** is its smallest unit (one or more containers run together), and a **service account** is the identity a pod runs as. On Amazon **EKS** (Elastic Kubernetes Service), **[IRSA](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/iam-roles-for-service-accounts.html)** (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) gives each Kubernetes service account its own IAM role, using the cluster's OIDC provider and the same `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` exchange. AWS lists the benefit as least privilege: "only Pods that use that service account have access to those permissions", instead of every pod sharing the node's instance role or a key in a secret. AWS's newer **EKS Pod Identity** does the same without a per-cluster OIDC provider.

The other clouds have direct equivalents: Azure **managed identities** with workload identity federation, and Google Cloud **Workload Identity Federation**, which Google says "eliminates the maintenance and security burden associated with service account keys".

The Tesla incident in 2018 shows the opposite. RedLock (a cloud security company) [found](https://web.archive.org/web/2018/https://redlock.io/blog/cryptojacking-tesla) Tesla's Kubernetes console on the internet without a password, and inside one pod, AWS credentials that reached an S3 bucket with telemetry data. Attackers used the cluster to mine cryptocurrency. Per-pod roles would not fix an open console, but cloud credentials stored in a pod turned one mistake into two.

blocks.question: An old role, created before IAM began rejecting this, trusts `token.actions.githubusercontent.com` with only the condition `aud = sts.amazonaws.com`. What is the risk?
options: GitHub cannot reach STS without a stored key
None, because aud proves the token came from your repository
Tokens will expire too quickly for deployments
Workflows in other people's repositories can obtain valid tokens with that audience and assume the role
blocks.explain: aud only says the token is meant for AWS STS. Any repository's workflow can request such a token. The sub condition is what ties the role to your repository and branch.

blocks.question: What does `permissions: id-token: write` in a GitHub Actions workflow do?
options: Gives the workflow write access to the repository
Lets the job request a signed OIDC token from GitHub; it grants no access to any resource by itself
Stores an AWS key in the repository
Disables token expiry
blocks.explain: GitHub's documentation says this setting only allows the workflow to fetch and use an OIDC token. Access to AWS comes from the role's trust policy accepting that token.

lessons.title: The same ideas in Azure and Google Cloud

blocks.md:
A security engineer is rarely lucky enough to use one cloud. A company might run its product on AWS, its staff identities in Microsoft Entra ID and a data team on Google Cloud. The good news: the ideas you have learned (a hierarchy of containers, principals, bundles of permissions, workload identities instead of keys, an audit log of control plane calls) exist in all three. The names and the shape of a grant differ.

The table below lines them up. Read it once now and come back to it when you meet an unfamiliar term at work.

blocks.code:
Idea                 AWS                        Azure                           Google Cloud
-------------------  -------------------------  ------------------------------  ------------------------------
Top of hierarchy     Organization + OUs         Management groups               Organization + folders
Isolation unit       Account                    Subscription, resource group    Project
Directory of people  IAM Identity Center/users  Microsoft Entra ID tenant       Cloud Identity / Workspace
Bundle of perms      Policy (JSON)              Role definition                 Role (set of permissions)
How a grant is made  Attach policy to identity  Role assignment: principal +    Role binding in an allow
                     (or name it in resource      role + scope                    policy on a resource
                     policy)
Workload identity    Role via instance profile, Managed identity (system- or    Service account attached
                     IRSA                       user-assigned)                  to the resource
Long-lived secret    IAM user access keys       Storage account keys, app       Service account keys
to avoid                                        client secrets
Keyless from outside OIDC provider +            Workload identity federation    Workload Identity Federation
                     AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity
Control plane log    CloudTrail (90-day         Activity log (kept 90 days)     Admin Activity audit logs
                     event history)                                             (always written)
blocks.caption: A comparison built from each provider's documentation. Simplified: each column has more features than fit here.

blocks.md:
**Azure.** Azure RBAC (role-based access control, the access control course's RBAC applied to Azure resources) grants access with a **role assignment**, which Microsoft defines as three elements: a **security principal** (a user, group, service principal, which is an app's identity in Entra ID, or managed identity), a **role definition** (a collection of permissions, such as the built-in Virtual Machine Contributor) and a **scope** (management group, subscription, resource group or resource). Assignments are inherited down the scopes.

Azure has two separate role systems, a frequent source of confusion. **Azure roles** control Azure resources (VMs, storage, databases). **Microsoft Entra roles** control the directory itself: creating users, resetting passwords, assigning admin roles. The person who creates a tenant becomes its **Global Administrator**, and a Global Administrator can elevate themselves to manage all Azure subscriptions in the tenant, so that role is as sensitive as an AWS management account.

blocks.title: An Azure role assignment, and how scope inheritance works

scenes.caption: A role assignment joins three things: who (a managed identity for an app), what (a role definition, here Storage Blob Data Reader) and where (a scope).
Assigned at the subscription scope, the role is inherited by every resource group and every storage account inside. Convenient, and far broader than one app needs.
Least privilege in Azure means choosing the narrowest scope: assign at the one storage account the app reads. The other resource group is untouched.

blocks.md:
**Managed identities** are Azure's workload identities. A **system-assigned** identity is created on one resource, such as a VM, and deleted with it; a **user-assigned** identity is a standalone resource that can be attached to several. Microsoft's summary of the benefit: "You don't need to manage credentials. Credentials aren't even accessible to you."

**Google Cloud.** IAM grants a **role** (a collection of permissions) to a **principal** through a **role binding** inside an **allow policy** attached to a resource, project, folder or organization, and bindings are inherited downwards. Workloads use **service accounts** attached to the resource. Google warns that "service account keys are a security risk if not managed correctly" and steers users to attached service accounts and Workload Identity Federation instead.

**Storm-0558, 2023.** Storm-0558 is Microsoft's name for a China-based threat actor (a group of attackers). It forged login tokens with an acquired Microsoft account (MSA, Microsoft's consumer login) signing key, and a token validation flaw let those consumer-signed tokens open enterprise mailboxes in Exchange Online, Microsoft's hosted email. Microsoft [says](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/msrc/blog/2023/07/microsoft-mitigates-china-based-threat-actor-storm-0558-targeting-of-customer-email) it began investigating on June 16, 2023 based on a customer's report of anomalous mail activity, and that about 25 organizations were affected. The cloud lesson: the identity provider's signing keys sit at the root of every cloud permission. When they fail, every policy in this course is bypassed, which is why cloud providers' own key management is part of your risk, and why a customer's own audit logs were what raised the alarm.

blocks.question: In Azure, an app's managed identity is given Storage Blob Data Reader at the subscription scope. What can it read?
options: Only the storage account it was created next to
Blob data in every storage account in that subscription, through inheritance
Nothing until a Microsoft Entra role is also assigned
Only blobs in the same region as the app
blocks.explain: Role assignments are inherited by everything below their scope. A subscription-scoped reader can read blob data in every storage account in the subscription. Assign at the narrowest scope that works.

blocks.question: Which Google Cloud practice matches AWS's advice to avoid long-lived IAM user access keys?
options: Grant every principal the Owner role
Download a service account key for each developer
Put keys in the project description
Use attached service accounts and Workload Identity Federation instead of service account keys
blocks.explain: Google calls service account keys a security risk and recommends attached service accounts or Workload Identity Federation, the same move from stored keys to short-lived credentials.

lessons.title: Storage exposure: public buckets, Block Public Access and SAS tokens

blocks.md:
A storage bucket is a folder in the cloud with a web address. If its policy says "anyone may read", then anyone on the internet who learns or guesses the name can download its contents, with no login and no hacking. Many of the largest data exposures of the last decade were exactly this: not a break-in, a door left open.

Each cloud has its own way of saying "anyone": `"Principal": "*"` in an S3 bucket policy (and the older AllUsers grant in S3 ACLs, access control lists), `allUsers` and `allAuthenticatedUsers` in Google Cloud Storage, and in Azure a SAS token URL that someone shares widely. This lesson takes them one at a time, with the guardrail each provider built on top.

blocks.caption: Vulnerable: Principal "*" with no condition means every person on the internet, signed in or not, may read every object.

Fixed: only one named role may read, and any request over plain HTTP is denied for everyone (aws:SecureTransport is false when TLS, Transport Layer Security, the encryption behind HTTPS, was not used). The bucket stays private, which AWS notes is the default for every new bucket and object.

blocks.md:
**S3 Block Public Access** is a guardrail that sits above bucket policies and ACLs. It has four settings:

- `BlockPublicAcls`: reject requests that would add a public ACL.
- `IgnorePublicAcls`: ignore any public ACLs that already exist.
- `BlockPublicPolicy`: reject a bucket policy that would grant public access.
- `RestrictPublicBuckets`: restrict access to buckets with public policies to AWS service principals and authorized users in the bucket owner's account.

They can be set for a whole organization, an account, a bucket or an access point, and S3 applies the most restrictive combination. Since April 2023 AWS turns on Block Public Access and disables ACLs for every new bucket by default. AWS's history note: buckets "have always been private by default"; Block Public Access arrived in 2018 and the option to disable ACLs in 2021.

blocks.title: Block Public Access in front of a public bucket policy

scenes.caption: Without Block Public Access, an anonymous request from anywhere reaches the bucket, the public policy allows GetObject, and the file is returned.
Account-level Block Public Access with RestrictPublicBuckets is turned on. The policy still says public, but S3 now ignores that grant for anyone outside the account.
With BlockPublicPolicy also on, a developer's attempt to save a new public policy is rejected outright, so the mistake never lands.
The report role inside the account is unaffected: guardrails stop public access without breaking the intended private grant.

blocks.md:
**Azure SAS tokens.** A SAS (shared access signature) is a signed URL that grants access to Azure Storage without an account login. URL fields say what it allows: `ss` (services), `srt` (resource types: s service, c container, o object), `sp` (permissions: r read, w write, d delete, l list), `se` (expiry), `sip` (allowed IPs) and `sig` (signature). An **account SAS** is signed with the storage account key; a **user delegation SAS** is signed with Microsoft Entra credentials, and Microsoft recommends it. Microsoft's documentation also warns: "It's not possible to audit the generation of SAS tokens."

**Microsoft AI research, 2023.** Wiz found that a public Microsoft GitHub repository, robust-models-transfer, told readers to download AI models from an Azure Storage URL with an account SAS. The token covered the whole storage account, not one container, granted "full control" rather than read-only, and was valid until 2051. Behind it sat 38 TB of other data, including backups of two employees' workstations with passwords, secret keys and over 30,000 internal Teams messages.

blocks.title: Two SAS tokens, field by field

scenes.caption: The fields of an account SAS URL. Each one narrows or widens what the link can do.
A token shaped like Microsoft's 2023 mistake: every resource type in the account, read, add, create, write, delete and list, expiring in 2051. It is as good as the account key.
A safer token: objects only, read only, valid for one hour, which is the lifetime Microsoft recommends as a maximum. Better still, a user delegation SAS signed with Entra credentials.

blocks.md:
Microsoft's account of the incident: Wiz reported it on June 22, 2023; Microsoft revoked the token and blocked external access by June 24. Microsoft said no customer data was exposed. Its own scanner had flagged this very URL earlier, but the finding was wrongly marked a false positive. Microsoft's recommended practice since: least privilege on every SAS, short lifetimes (one hour or less), treat SAS URLs as secrets, have a revocation plan (stored access policies, or rotating the account key), set a SAS expiration policy on the storage account, and monitor storage logs.

**Google Cloud Storage** uses IAM grants to `allUsers` (anyone on the internet) and `allAuthenticatedUsers` (anyone signed in to any Google account, which is nearly everyone). **Public access prevention**, when enforced on a bucket or across a project or organization, makes requests authorized through those two principals fail, the equivalent of S3 Block Public Access.

Turn on the provider's public-access guardrail at the highest level you can (organization or account), and treat any exception as a reviewed, documented decision. Then scan for anything public anyway: IAM Access Analyzer in AWS reports buckets shared publicly or with other accounts.

blocks.question: A bucket has a policy with `"Principal": "*"` allowing GetObject, but account-level Block Public Access has `RestrictPublicBuckets` turned on. An anonymous user requests an object. What happens?
options: The bucket policy is deleted automatically
The object is returned, because the bucket policy allows it
Only the first object is returned
Access is denied: the public grant is restricted to principals in the owner's account and AWS services
blocks.explain: RestrictPublicBuckets limits access to a bucket with a public policy to AWS service principals and authorized users in the owning account. The policy text remains but no longer opens the bucket to the world.

blocks.question: Why was the 2023 Microsoft SAS token so dangerous compared with a typical shared link?
options: It was signed with a weak hash
It used HTTP instead of HTTPS
It covered the whole storage account with full control and expired in 2051, and SAS creation is not logged, so nobody could see it existed
It required MFA that attackers could bypass
blocks.explain: Scope (whole account), permissions (full control) and lifetime (decades) made it equivalent to the account key, and because SAS generation cannot be audited, the owners had no inventory of it.

lessons.title: Secrets and keys: KMS, envelope encryption and secret stores

blocks.md:
Uber's 2016 breach had a detail that made it worse: the files the intruders downloaded were database backups stored "in clear, readable text, rather than encrypting the information", in the FTC's words. Encryption at rest would not have stopped someone holding a key that could also decrypt, but it changes the question from "who can read this bucket?" to "who can read this bucket **and** use this encryption key?", two permissions that can be granted separately and logged separately.

Two cloud services carry that idea: a **key management service** that holds encryption keys and never lets them out, and a **secrets manager** that holds passwords and API keys so they stop living in code.

**AWS KMS** (Key Management Service) keeps **KMS keys** that "can't be downloaded": every use is an API call that IAM checks and CloudTrail records. KMS keys also have a **key policy**, and AWS's evaluation rules make it special: like a role trust policy, a KMS key policy must explicitly allow access.

Sending gigabytes to KMS for every operation would be slow, so systems use **[envelope encryption](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/kms-cryptography.html)**. KMS's `GenerateDataKey` call returns a fresh **data key** twice: once in plaintext, for immediate use, and once encrypted under the KMS key. You encrypt the data locally with the plaintext data key, throw that copy away, and store the encrypted data key next to the ciphertext, which AWS's cryptography documentation calls packaging the encrypted key and the ciphertext into a single structure, an envelope. To read it later, you ask KMS to decrypt the small data key, then decrypt the data locally. AWS notes that KMS "does not store, manage, or track your data keys".

blocks.title: Envelope encryption with a KMS key

scenes.caption: The app asks KMS for a data key under the KMS key named for customer data. IAM and the key policy must both allow kms:GenerateDataKey.
The app encrypts the record locally with the plaintext data key, then forgets that key. Only the wrapped (encrypted) copy is kept, stored next to the ciphertext.
Reading it back: fetch the object, send only the small wrapped key to KMS, get the plaintext data key back, decrypt locally.
Someone with only S3 read permission gets ciphertext and a wrapped key, and their Decrypt call is refused. Reading the data needs a second, separate permission, and the attempt is logged.

blocks.code:
import os
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM

# Stand-in for the KMS key: in real KMS this key never leaves the service.
kms_key = AESGCM.generate_key(bit_length=256)

def generate_data_key():
    data_key = AESGCM.generate_key(bit_length=256)
    nonce = os.urandom(12)
    wrapped = nonce + AESGCM(kms_key).encrypt(nonce, data_key, None)
    return data_key, wrapped          # plaintext copy, encrypted copy

def kms_decrypt(wrapped):
    return AESGCM(kms_key).decrypt(wrapped[:12], wrapped[12:], None)

# Encrypt: use the plaintext data key, keep only the wrapped copy.
data_key, wrapped_key = generate_data_key()
nonce = os.urandom(12)
ciphertext = AESGCM(data_key).encrypt(nonce, b"card=4111...;name=Ana", None)
del data_key
envelope = {"wrapped_key": wrapped_key, "nonce": nonce, "ciphertext": ciphertext}

# Decrypt: ask "KMS" to unwrap the data key, then decrypt locally.
key = kms_decrypt(envelope["wrapped_key"])
print(AESGCM(key).decrypt(envelope["nonce"], envelope["ciphertext"], None))
print(len(wrapped_key), "bytes of wrapped key stored next to the data")
blocks.caption: A runnable local model using AES-GCM (Advanced Encryption Standard in Galois/Counter Mode, which also detects tampering). A local key stands in for the KMS key, which in real KMS never leaves the service. Output: the record, then 60 bytes of wrapped key (12-byte nonce, 32-byte key, 16-byte tag).

blocks.md:
S3 does this for you with **SSE-KMS** (server-side encryption with KMS keys). AWS documents the consequence that matters for security: to upload an object encrypted under a KMS key you need `kms:GenerateDataKey`, and to download one you need `kms:Decrypt` on that key, in addition to the S3 permissions. A role that can read a bucket but not use its key gets nothing readable.

**Secret stores.** AWS **Secrets Manager** stores database passwords, API keys and OAuth tokens and can rotate them on a schedule; AWS says it means "you no longer need hard-coded credentials in application source code". **Azure Key Vault** stores secrets, keys and certificates, and lets vault owners set up auditing of who accesses them. The application fetches the secret at runtime using its role or managed identity, so the only thing in the code is the secret's name.

blocks.code:
import json
import boto3

# Bad: the password lives in the source code and in every copy of the repo
# DB_PASSWORD = "Winter2024!"

# Better: fetch it at runtime with the role's permissions
client = boto3.client("secretsmanager", region_name="us-east-1")
resp = client.get_secret_value(SecretId="prod/shop/db")
creds = json.loads(resp["SecretString"])     # {"username": ..., "password": ...}
blocks.caption: The password moves out of the repository. Access to it is now an IAM permission on one secret, every read is in CloudTrail, and rotation does not need a code change.

blocks.md: Encryption at rest only protects you from people who cannot use the key. If the same over-broad role can both read the bucket and call Decrypt, as an application role often can, the encryption adds an audit trail but no barrier. Grant `kms:Decrypt` as narrowly as the data itself.

blocks.question: A bucket uses SSE-KMS with a customer-managed key. A role has `s3:GetObject` on the bucket but no permission to use the key. What happens when it downloads an object?
options: It gets the plaintext, because S3 decrypts automatically
S3 returns a random key
It gets the ciphertext and can decrypt it offline
The download fails, because reading an SSE-KMS object also requires kms:Decrypt on the key
blocks.explain: S3 must decrypt the data key through KMS on the caller's behalf, which requires kms:Decrypt. Without it the request is denied, so the key is a second, independent gate.

blocks.question: In envelope encryption, what is stored next to the encrypted data?
options: The KMS key itself
The data key encrypted under the KMS key
The plaintext data key
Nothing; KMS stores every data key
blocks.explain: The plaintext data key is used and discarded. The wrapped copy is stored with the ciphertext, and only someone allowed to call Decrypt on the KMS key can unwrap it. KMS does not store data keys.

lessons.title: Network controls: VPCs, security groups and private endpoints

blocks.md:
Lesson 1 said identity is the main perimeter, but the network still matters in two ways. It decides which of your servers the internet can reach at all, and it can decide where your credentials are allowed to be used from. A database that only accepts connections from the web servers cannot be guessed at from a coffee shop, and a bucket that only answers requests from your own network ignores stolen keys used from anywhere else.

A **VPC** (virtual private cloud) is a private network you define inside AWS: an address range split into **subnets**, with route tables deciding which subnets can reach the internet. Azure's equivalent is the **virtual network** (VNet).

**Security groups** are AWS's firewall for each instance (and other resources such as databases). Two properties matter:

- You "can specify allow rules, but not deny rules". Everything not allowed is blocked.
- They are **stateful**: if a request is allowed in, the response is allowed out automatically, and vice versa.
